title: Noncardiogenic Pulmonary Edema -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Noncardiogenic pulmonary edema is a clinical syndrome characterized by the acute accumulation of fluid in the alveolar and interstitial spaces, resulting from increased capillary permeability rather than elevated hydrostatic pressure. The condition arises in diverse settings, including acute respiratory distress syndrome, sepsis, transfusion-related acute lung injury, high-altitude exposure, and neurogenic injury. Patients typically present with dyspnea, hypoxemia, and diffuse pulmonary infiltrates on chest imaging that resemble cardiogenic pulmonary edema but occur in the absence of elevated pulmonary capillary wedge pressure. Pathophysiologic mechanisms involve inflammatory injury to the alveolar-capillary barrier, cytokine release, and endothelial disruption. Without prompt recognition and treatment, noncardiogenic pulmonary edema can progress to respiratory failure, multiorgan dysfunction, and death. Supportive care, including oxygen therapy, mechanical ventilation strategies such as low tidal volume ventilation, and prone positioning, is essential to improve gas exchange and limit ventilator-induced lung injury. Definitive management requires addressing the underlying cause.

title: Noncardiogenic Pulmonary Edema -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This continuing education activity enhances participant knowledge and competence in recognizing, diagnosing, and managing noncardiogenic pulmonary edema. Learners gain the ability to differentiate this entity from cardiogenic pulmonary edema through history, physical examination, laboratory testing, and hemodynamic assessment. Instruction emphasizes evidence-based ventilation strategies, pharmacologic considerations, and the importance of early monitoring for complications such as ventilator-induced lung injury and multiorgan failure. Collaboration among interprofessional team members—including emergency clinicians, intensivists, respiratory therapists, radiologists, nurses, and allied health professionals—is highlighted as critical to timely diagnosis, delivery of supportive care, and coordination of patient-centered management. By strengthening communication and teamwork across specialties, participants will develop the skills needed to optimize patient safety, reduce morbidity and mortality, and improve overall outcomes in patients with noncardiogenic pulmonary edema.

title: Noncardiogenic Pulmonary Edema -- Introduction
content: Pulmonary edema is caused by fluid accumulation in the lung parenchyma. This impairs gas exchange and leads to rapid deterioration in respiratory status, which can result in respiratory failure if unaddressed. The condition has multiple etiologies, which can be separated into cardiogenic and noncardiogenic causes. Noncardiogenic pulmonary edema is an inflammatory process that increases pulmonary capillary permeability, allowing fluid to move into the pulmonary and interstitial spaces, disrupting gas exchange and lung function.

title: Noncardiogenic Pulmonary Edema -- Introduction
content: Conversely, cardiogenic pulmonary edema results from left-sided congestive heart failure, leading to elevated pulmonary venous pressures. [1] The distinction can be made by history, physical examination, and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure measurement, which is elevated (>18 mm Hg) in cardiogenic but not noncardiogenic pulmonary edema. [2] [3] Pulmonary edema requires prompt recognition and management tailored to the underlying cause.

title: Noncardiogenic Pulmonary Edema -- Etiology
content: The primary causes of noncardiogenic pulmonary edema include: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) (Please see StatPearls' companion resource, " Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome, " for more information. Neurogenic pulmonary edema) High altitude pulmonary edema (HAPE) Drugs and toxins (opioid overdose, contrast agents, salicylate toxicity) Pulmonary embolism Transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI) Pulmonary veno-occlusive disease Viral infections Preeclampsia and eclampsia Negative-pressure pulmonary edema Reperfusion pulmonary edema Re-expansion pulmonary edema Capillary leak syndrome Uremic lung [2] [4] [5] The acronym "NOT-CARDIAC" is used to aid recall: N: Near-drowning O: Oxygen therapy, postintubation T: Trauma, transfusion-related C: Central nervous system causes (neurogenic pulmonary edema) A: Allergic alveolitis R: Renal failure D: Drugs I: Inhaled toxins A: Altitude (HAPE), ARDS C: Contusion [1] [6]

title: Noncardiogenic Pulmonary Edema -- Epidemiology
content: Most etiologies of noncardiogenic pulmonary edema are rare but should be considered as part of a broad differential diagnosis. ARDS affects approximately 200,000 patients in the United States each year, resulting in 74,500 deaths. Approximately 25% of ARDS cases are classified as mild, while the remaining 75% are moderate or severe, defined by the partial pressure of oxygen to fraction of inspired oxygen ratio (PaO 2 /FiO 2) . [7] ARDS accounts for 10% of intensive care unit admissions worldwide and has a mortality rate of 35% to 46%. [8] [9]

title: Noncardiogenic Pulmonary Edema -- Epidemiology
content: HAPE is a rare condition that lacks a systematic epidemiologic analysis; however, individuals ascending to altitudes higher than 2250 meters are at increased risk of developing HAPE. [10] TRALI is the leading cause of death related to blood transfusion, as documented by the US Food and Drug Administration. Patients with critical illnesses are at greater risk because they often require more transfused blood products, and the incidence is 1 per 5000 units of packed red blood cells administered. Please see StatPearls' companion resource, " Transfusion-Associated Acute Lung Injury, " for more information.

title: Noncardiogenic Pulmonary Edema -- Pathophysiology
content: Normally, a continuous exchange of liquid and colloids occurs between the vascular bed and interstitial space, and the lymphatic system continuously removes excess fluid. Noncardiogenic pulmonary edema is caused by an inflammatory response that damages the alveolar capillary membrane, increasing its permeability. [2] [11] Pulmonary capillary leak, as postulated by the “blast theory,” leads to increased pulmonary permeability.

title: Noncardiogenic Pulmonary Edema -- Pathophysiology
content: This permeability is mediated by the excess release of cytokines and endothelin, oxidative stress, and apoptosis, all within a milieu of dysregulated inflammation that disrupts endothelial cells and breaks down the alveolar capillary barrier. [12] [13] [14] The pulmonary interstitial protein concentration exceeds that of plasma by more than 60%, [5] governed by the Starling principle. As pulmonary edema accumulates, the surface area available for gas exchange is reduced, impairing ventilation-perfusion matching and resulting in hypoxia and respiratory failure. Moreover, abnormal deposition of extracellular matrix and fibrosis further impede lung compliance. [12]

title: Noncardiogenic Pulmonary Edema -- History and Physical
content: The presentation of cardiogenic and noncardiogenic pulmonary edema is similar, with dyspnea as the primary symptom. The onset ranges from a few hours to several days, depending on the etiology. A history of worsening respiratory status and increasing hypoxia may include increased work of breathing, dizziness, headache, altered mental status, and central or peripheral cyanosis. Concurrent disease processes known to cause ARDS should be identified, such as sepsis, pancreatitis, pneumonia, or trauma. Thoracic surgery, cardiopulmonary bypass, recent blood transfusion, high altitude exposure, risk factors for pulmonary embolism, and drug exposures, specifically opioid and salicylate use, are rarer causes of noncardiogenic pulmonary edema.

title: Noncardiogenic Pulmonary Edema -- History and Physical
content: The physical examination may be unremarkable in noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, but it can be used to exclude a cardiogenic source. The absence of left-sided heart murmurs and a third heart sound (S3 gallop), along with normal fluid balance, nondistended neck veins, and the absence of peripheral edema, are findings consistent with noncardiogenic pulmonary edema. [15] Chest auscultation may reveal fine inspiratory crackles or bronchial breath sounds, depending on the degree of edema. General examination findings of hypoxia, including confusion, irritability, cyanosis, elevated respiratory rate, and tachycardia, may also be present.

title: Noncardiogenic Pulmonary Edema -- Evaluation -- Laboratory Testing
content: Complete blood count test to identify infection or sepsis Arterial blood gas testing to evaluate the PaO 2 /FiO 2 ratio and degree of hypoxia Lipase and amylase serum levels to identify pancreatitis Brain-type natriuretic peptide, troponin, and renal function tests to evaluate for cardiogenic pulmonary edema

title: Noncardiogenic Pulmonary Edema -- Evaluation -- Radiologic Testing
content: Chest radiography: A classic batwing pattern of pulmonary opacities is observed. Cardiomegaly, vascular redistribution, pleural effusion, septal lines, and mediastinal widening are usually absent. [1] [16] A patchy distribution of edema with air bronchograms and peripheral ground-glass opacities may also be present. (See Image. Noncardiogenic Pulmonary Edema, Chest Radiograph). Due to significant overlap in imaging findings, advanced imaging techniques, such as high-resolution CT and point-of-care ultrasound, are often required. [17] [18]

title: Noncardiogenic Pulmonary Edema -- Evaluation -- Echocardiography
content: This is used to assess left ventricular ejection fraction and valvular function; acute systolic and diastolic function changes can also be identified.

title: Noncardiogenic Pulmonary Edema -- Evaluation -- Pulmonary Artery Catheterization
content: Considered the gold standard for identifying the cause of pulmonary edema. A pulmonary artery catheter is inserted into a central vein and advanced through the right side of the heart into a pulmonary artery. The measurement provides definitive confirmation by identifying pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) <18 mm Hg, which excludes a cardiogenic source of pulmonary edema.

title: Noncardiogenic Pulmonary Edema -- Evaluation -- Essentials in Diagnosis:
content: Bilateral diffuse alveolar infiltrates with severe hypoxemia PCWP <18 mm Hg PaO 2 /FiO 2 ratio <200 mm Hg

title: Noncardiogenic Pulmonary Edema -- Treatment / Management
content: The treatment of noncardiogenic pulmonary edema primarily involves addressing the underlying pathophysiologic mechanisms. [5] There is no direct treatment for the inflammatory process driving increased vascular permeability at the alveolar capillary membrane. Supportive therapy corrects hypoxia and minimizes lung injury. The degree of respiratory support required primarily depends on analyzing arterial blood gases and the patient's breathing work.

title: Noncardiogenic Pulmonary Edema -- Treatment / Management
content: Hypoxemia (PaO 2 <60 mm Hg) without hypercapnia can be treated by increasing the FiO 2 , which can be administered via nasal prongs, a Hudson mask, or a Venturi mask, depending on the level of oxygen delivery required to elevate the PaO 2 . A trial of noninvasive ventilation can be considered if there are no contraindications. Mechanical ventilation is necessary if a PaO2 greater than 60 mm Hg cannot be achieved or the patient develops fatigue due to progressive hypercapnia.

title: Noncardiogenic Pulmonary Edema -- Treatment / Management
content: Mechanical ventilation strategies have been developed to prevent ventilator-induced lung injury, a particular concern in ARDS. Given the heterogeneous pattern of lung involvement, volumes delivered via mechanical ventilation are not distributed equally, leaving the unaffected alveoli susceptible to overdistension and damage. [19] Low tidal volume ventilation (4–6 mL/kg predicted body weight) and higher positive end-expiratory pressure (10-15 mm Hg) are the primary strategies used in ventilating patients with ARDS. [20] [21]

title: Noncardiogenic Pulmonary Edema -- Treatment / Management
content: Prone positioning has also been shown to improve alveolar recruitment and enhance oxygenation. [22] Systemic corticosteroids have been extensively studied due to their anti-inflammatory effects. Current evidence suggests that the duration of mechanical ventilation and mortality can be reduced when treatment is initiated early. However, no particular corticosteroid has demonstrated superiority.

title: Noncardiogenic Pulmonary Edema -- Treatment / Management
content: Despite these strategies, there is a risk of ventilator-induced lung injury. A newer intervention that may prevent barotrauma is extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. [23] Inhaled nitric oxide, prostacyclins, statins, aspirin, fluid restriction, and high-frequency ventilation have not improved patient outcomes. [22] Investigational therapies include mesenchymal stem cells, gene-editing approaches (such as CRISPR/Cas9), and immunotherapy (including immune checkpoint inhibitors and cytokine antagonist medications). [12] Other causes of noncardiogenic pulmonary edema are managed with supportive care, including supplemental oxygen or mechanical ventilation, along with treatment of the inciting cause.

title: Noncardiogenic Pulmonary Edema -- Differential Diagnosis
content: The differential diagnosis for noncardiogenic pulmonary edema includes: Cardiogenic pulmonary edema is characterized by increased brain natriuretic peptide levels, reduced left-ventricular ejection fraction, cardiomegaly, Kerley B lines, interlobular septal thickening, and central distribution on high-resolution CT, as well as pleural effusion. (See StatPearls' companion resource, " Cardiogenic Pulmonary Edema ," for more information.) Acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease Lymphangitic carcinomatosis (See StatPearls' companion resource, " Lymphangitic Carcinomatosis, " for more information.) Re-expansion pulmonary edema Diffuse pulmonary hemorrhage Diffuse pulmonary infection Vasculitis Eosinophilic pneumonitis Aspiration pneumonitis Atelectasis [24] [25]

title: Noncardiogenic Pulmonary Edema -- Prognosis
content: The prognosis varies according to the cause of noncardiogenic pulmonary edema. The mortality rate of ARDS ranges from 35% to 46%. [8] Prognosis is poor in neurogenic pulmonary edema; more than 70% of cases occur following intracranial hemorrhage, and 3% following seizure. [26] Patients with a history of HAPE who ascend above 4500 meters have a 60% chance of recurrence. [27] Reperfusion pulmonary edema accounts for 25% of the mortality following lung transplantation. [28] Mortality from TRALI ranges from 5% to 8%; however, it increases in patients with critical illness to 60%. [29] [30]

title: Noncardiogenic Pulmonary Edema -- Complications
content: The most important complication from noncardiogenic pulmonary edema is respiratory failure, necessitating endotracheal intubation. Given the difficulties with ventilating heterogeneous lungs, this intervention exposes patients to the risk of ventilator-induced lung injury. Progression of noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, if not diagnosed and treated promptly, can worsen disease severity and require prolonged mechanical ventilation and intensive care. The degree of hypoxia caused by noncardiogenic pulmonary edema increases the risk of arrhythmias, pulmonary hypertension, right heart strain, hypoxic brain injury, and multiorgan failure.

title: Noncardiogenic Pulmonary Edema -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Patients with a history of HAPE should be educated about the risk of reoccurrence with rapid ascent to high altitude. Patients at risk of aspiration should be fed with the head of the bed elevated to prevent aspiration. Patients with conditions associated with noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, including sepsis, pancreatitis, pneumonia, and those receiving blood transfusions, should be monitored closely for signs of hypoxia or respiratory distress.

title: Noncardiogenic Pulmonary Edema -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Noncardiogenic pulmonary edema needs to be recognized and treated promptly to avoid the complications of hypoxia and respiratory failure. Early recognition may involve emergency medicine clinicians, nurses monitoring patients during blood transfusions, or intensivists caring for patients at high risk of complications. Education regarding the signs and symptoms of noncardiogenic pulmonary edema and its distinct differences from cardiogenic pulmonary edema is vital, given the differences in treatment. Following diagnosis, a well-coordinated, interdisciplinary approach including intensivists, radiologists, respiratory specialists, nurses, and allied health professionals is needed to optimize patient outcomes.
